topics.title: Verbs and Tenses
topics.description: Using simple, continuous and perfect tenses to show when actions happen.

lessons.title: Simple Present and Simple Past
objectives: Use the simple present for habits, facts and timetables
Use the simple past for completed actions
Form regular and irregular past tense verbs
Make negatives and questions with do, does and did
lessons.intro: A verb tells us what someone does, and its tense tells us when. 'She walks to school' describes a habit; 'She walked to school yesterday' describes a finished action in the past. The simple present and simple past are the tenses we use most often in speaking and writing. Getting them right makes your English clear and correct.
sections: The simple present

We use the simple present for habits and routines ('I brush my teeth twice a day'), general truths and facts ('Water boils at 100 °C'; 'The Earth goes round the Sun'), and fixed timetables ('The train leaves at 6:15'). With he, she, it or a singular noun, add -s or -es to the verb: she reads, he watches, the dog barks. Verbs ending in consonant + y change y to ies: he studies. Signal words include always, usually, often, every day and never. The verb 'have' becomes 'has' and 'be' becomes am, is or are.
The simple past

We use the simple past for actions completed at a definite time in the past: 'We visited Jaipur last summer.' Regular verbs add -ed (play, played; stop, stopped; carry, carried). Many common verbs are irregular and must be learnt: go, went; see, saw; eat, ate; write, wrote; buy, bought; take, took; think, thought. The past of be is was (I, he, she, it) or were (you, we, they). Signal words include yesterday, last week, ago and in 2019.
Negatives and questions

In the simple present, use do not (don't) or does not (doesn't) with the base form of the verb: 'He does not like spicy food' (not 'does not likes'). Questions begin with do or does: 'Do you play chess?' 'Does she live here?' In the simple past, use did not (didn't) and did for all subjects, again with the base form: 'They did not come.' 'Did you finish your homework?' A very common mistake is to use the past form after did: 'Did you went?' is wrong; say 'Did you go?'
definitions: Tense
The form of a verb that shows the time of an action.
Simple present
The tense used for habits, facts and timetables.
Simple past
The tense used for actions completed at a definite past time.
Irregular verb
A verb that does not form its past tense by adding -ed.
Base form
The plain form of a verb, such as go, eat, write.
examples: My grandmother tells us a story every night. (habit)
Neil Armstrong walked on the Moon in 1969. (completed past action)

worked.problem: Correct the errors: 'Yesterday my brother go to the market and buyed apples. He don't like oranges. Did he paid?'
steps: 'Yesterday' shows past time: go → went; 'buyed' → bought (irregular).
'He' needs does in the negative: don't → doesn't (present habit).
After did use the base form: paid → pay.
worked.answer: Yesterday my brother went to the market and bought apples. He doesn't like oranges. Did he pay?

lessons.real_world: News reports describe events in the simple past ('The rocket launched at 10 a.m.'), while timetables, product instructions and science facts use the simple present. Diary entries and travel blogs are mostly written in the simple past.
takeaways: Simple present: habits, facts and timetables; add -s/-es for he, she, it.
Simple past: completed actions at a definite past time.
Learn common irregular past forms.
After do, does and did always use the base form of the verb.
practice: Fill in: The Sun ___ (rise) in the east.
Make a question: She watched the match.

EASY: Choose the correct form: 'She ___ to school every day.'
What is the past tense of 'write'?
The simple past of write is wrote.
Which sentence states a general truth?
A scientific fact is expressed in the simple present.
Did + base form: Did you see the film?
MEDIUM: Choose the correct negative: 'He likes tea.'
Fill in: 'Last year we ___ (visit) the Taj Mahal.'
What is the past tense of 'carry'?
Change y to i and add -ed: carried.
Fill in: 'The bus ___ at 7:30 tomorrow morning.' (timetable)
Fixed timetables use the simple present.
Timetables use the simple present even for the future: leaves.
HARD: Find the error: 'My father reads the newspaper every morning and drinked tea.'
It is a habit and the verb is irregular anyway.
The habit needs 'drinks'; 'drinked' is not a word.
She didn't went to the party.
She don't went to the party.
She didn't go to the party.
She not go to the party.
The negative past is didn't + go.
Which sentence uses the simple past correctly?
We bought a new bicycle two days ago.
We buy a new bicycle two days ago.
We buyed a new bicycle two days ago.
We have buy a new bicycle two days ago.
'Two days ago' is a definite past time.
Bought is the correct irregular past form.
Choose the correct question for: 'They study in the library.'
Does they study in the library?
Did they studies in the library?
Do they studies in the library?
Do they study in the library?
Do + they + base form: Do they study?

lessons.title: Continuous and Perfect Tenses
objectives: Form and use the present and past continuous tenses
Form and use the present perfect tense
Distinguish the present perfect from the simple past
Use since and for correctly
lessons.intro: Compare 'I read a book', 'I am reading a book' and 'I have read this book'. The first is a simple fact or completed action; the second describes an action in progress now; the third connects a past action to the present. Continuous tenses show actions in progress, and perfect tenses show completed actions with a link to a later time. Using them correctly adds precision to your writing.
sections: Continuous tenses

The present continuous is formed with am, is or are + the -ing form of the verb: 'She is cooking dinner.' It describes actions happening now, temporary situations ('He is staying with us this week') and planned future arrangements ('We are meeting at five'). The past continuous is formed with was or were + -ing: 'I was reading when the lights went out.' It describes an action in progress at a past moment, often interrupted by a shorter action in the simple past. Some verbs of feeling and knowing, such as know, like, want and believe, are not usually used in continuous forms: say 'I know the answer', not 'I am knowing'.
The present perfect

The present perfect is formed with has or have + the past participle: 'I have finished my homework.' Past participles of regular verbs end in -ed, but irregular verbs have their own forms: go, went, gone; see, saw, seen; write, wrote, written; eat, ate, eaten. The present perfect is used for past actions whose results matter now ('She has lost her key, so she cannot open the door'), for experiences ('Have you ever been to Kerala?'), and for actions that began in the past and continue now ('We have lived here since 2015').
Present perfect or simple past? Since or for?

Use the simple past when the time of the action is stated or finished: 'I saw that film last week.' Use the present perfect when no finished time is mentioned: 'I have seen that film.' Never use the present perfect with yesterday, last year or ago: 'I have seen it yesterday' is wrong. With the present perfect, since shows the starting point (since Monday, since 2010, since I was five), while for shows the length of time (for three days, for ten years). So: 'She has taught here for twelve years' and 'She has taught here since 2013'.
definitions: Present continuous
am/is/are + verb-ing; an action happening now.
Past continuous
was/were + verb-ing; an action in progress in the past.
Present perfect
has/have + past participle; a past action linked to the present.
Past participle
The verb form used in perfect tenses, e.g. written, gone, played.
examples: Look! The children are flying kites. (now)
I have just finished my project. (recent action, result now)

worked.problem: Choose and explain: 'While I (walked / was walking) home, it (started / was starting) to rain.'
steps: Walking home was a longer action in progress → past continuous: was walking.
The rain began at one moment and interrupted it → simple past: started.
worked.answer: While I was walking home, it started to rain.

worked.problem: Fill in since or for: 'He has been ill ___ Monday' and 'We have waited ___ two hours.'
steps: Monday is a starting point → since.
Two hours is a length of time → for.

lessons.real_world: Live cricket commentary uses the present continuous ('He is running in to bowl'), while news headlines and reports on recent events often use the present perfect ('Scientists have discovered a new species'). Job applications use the present perfect for experience: 'I have worked as a volunteer for two years.'
takeaways: Continuous tenses: be + verb-ing for actions in progress.
Past continuous is often interrupted by a simple past action.
Present perfect: has/have + past participle, linking the past to now.
Since = starting point; for = length of time; no present perfect with 'yesterday' or 'ago'.
practice: Fill in: They ___ (play) cricket at this moment.
Write the past participle of 'take', 'go' and 'eat'.
Correct: 'I have visited Agra last year.'

EASY: Choose the present continuous: 'Look! The baby ___.'
is + sleeping shows an action in progress now.
Fill in: 'We have lived here ___ ten years.'
Ten years is a length of time.
Choose the past continuous: 'At 8 p.m. yesterday, I ___ dinner.'
In progress at a past moment.
was + eating shows an action in progress at that time.
MEDIUM: Verbs of knowing use simple forms: I know.
I saw that film last week.
I have seen that film last week.
I have saw that film last week.
I seen that film last week.
A finished time takes the simple past.
Fill in: 'When the phone rang, I ___ a bath.'
The bath was in progress when interrupted.
Past continuous for the longer interrupted action.
HARD: Which sentence uses the present perfect for an experience?
Have you ever climbed a mountain?
I was climbing when it snowed.
'Have you ever…' asks about experiences up to now.
Find the error: 'She has gone to the market an hour ago.'
Present perfect cannot be used with 'ago'.
With 'an hour ago' use the simple past: She went…
Choose the correct pair: 'While they ___ football, the ball ___ the window.'
Past continuous for the game; simple past for the sudden break.
Which sentence shows a past action with a result now?
I lose my wallet every day.
I have lost my wallet, so I can't pay.
The present perfect links the loss to the present problem.

topics.title: Words in Context
topics.description: Building words with prefixes and suffixes and working out meanings from context.

lessons.title: Prefixes and Suffixes
objectives: Identify root words, prefixes and suffixes
Use common prefixes to change meaning
Use suffixes to change word class
Apply spelling rules when adding suffixes
lessons.intro: Many long English words are built from smaller parts. 'Unbreakable' is made from the root 'break', the prefix 'un-' meaning not, and the suffix '-able' meaning able to be. If you know the meaning of common word parts, you can often work out the meaning of a word you have never seen before. Word building is one of the fastest ways to grow your vocabulary.
sections: Roots and prefixes

The root (or base) word carries the main meaning. A prefix is added to the front of a root and changes its meaning. Common prefixes include un-, in-, im-, dis- and non- (not): unfair, invisible, impatient, dislike, non-stop; re- (again): rewrite, rebuild; pre- (before): preview, prepaid; mis- (wrongly): misspell, misunderstand; over- (too much): overcook; sub- (under): submarine, subway; inter- (between): international; and multi- (many): multicoloured. Prefixes never change the spelling of the root: dis + satisfied = dissatisfied, mis + spell = misspell, with double letters.
Suffixes and word class

A suffix is added to the end of a word and often changes its word class. Suffixes that make nouns include -ness (kindness), -ment (enjoyment), -tion/-sion (creation, decision), -ity (activity) and -er/-or (teacher, actor). Suffixes that make adjectives include -ful (hopeful), -less (careless), -able/-ible (washable, visible), -ous (dangerous) and -ive (creative). The suffix -ly usually turns an adjective into an adverb (quick, quickly), and -ify, -ise and -en make verbs (simplify, modernise, widen). One root can produce a whole family: care, careful, carefully, careless, carelessness, caring.
Spelling rules

When a suffix beginning with a vowel is added to a word ending in silent e, drop the e: make, making; hope, hoping; but keep it before a consonant suffix: hopeful, careless. For words ending in consonant + y, change y to i before most suffixes: happy, happiness; beauty, beautiful; but keep y before -ing: carrying. For short words with one vowel followed by one consonant, double the consonant before a vowel suffix: run, running; stop, stopped; big, bigger. Checking a dictionary is wise for tricky words.
definitions: Root word
The basic word to which prefixes and suffixes are added.
Prefix
Letters added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning.
Suffix
Letters added to the end of a word, often changing its word class.
Word family
Words built from the same root, such as act, action, active, actor.
examples: Re + view = review (look at again); pre + view = preview (look at before).

steps: disagreement = dis- (not) + agree (root) + -ment (noun suffix): the state of not agreeing.
unbelievable = un- (not) + believe (root) + -able (can be): believe loses its e before -able.
Meaning: not able to be believed.
worked.answer: Disagreement: the state of not agreeing. Unbelievable: impossible to believe.

lessons.real_world: Scientific and medical words are built from prefixes and roots: 'hyper-tension' (high blood pressure) and 'sub-marine' (under the sea). Knowing word parts helps you understand new terms in science textbooks, news reports and instructions.
takeaways: Prefixes change meaning; suffixes often change word class.
Learn common prefixes: un-, dis-, re-, pre-, mis-, sub-, inter-.
Learn common suffixes: -ness, -ment, -tion, -ful, -less, -able, -ly.
Follow spelling rules: drop silent e, change y to i, double the final consonant.
practice: Add a prefix to make the opposite of 'honest'.
Make a noun from 'kind' and an adjective from 'danger'.

EASY: What does the prefix 're-' mean in 'rewrite'?
Re- means again: rewrite means write again.
Which suffix turns 'care' into an adjective meaning 'without care'?
Which word has a prefix meaning 'before'?
MEDIUM: Prefixes do not change the root.
Submerge means to go or put under water.
Which suffix makes 'simple' into a verb?
HARD: In 'The instructions were incomprehensible', the word means:
It means not able to be understood.
Which pair belongs to the same word family?
Short word, one vowel + one consonant.
Double the final consonant: stop → stopping.

lessons.title: Using Context Clues
objectives: Explain what context clues are
Use definition, synonym, antonym and example clues
Infer the meaning of unfamiliar words from the sentence
Check guesses with a dictionary
lessons.intro: When reading, you will often meet words you do not know. Stopping to look up every word breaks the flow of reading. Good readers first use the words and sentences around an unfamiliar word, called its context, to make an intelligent guess about its meaning. Writers often leave clues on purpose, especially in textbooks. Learning to spot these clues will make you a faster and more confident reader.
sections: Definition and synonym clues

Sometimes the writer explains the word directly. In 'An archipelago, a group of islands, lies off the coast', the meaning is given between commas. Signal words for definitions include 'is', 'means', 'refers to', 'that is' and 'or'. A synonym clue gives a word with a similar meaning nearby: 'The hikers were exhausted; they were so tired they could barely walk.' Here 'so tired' explains 'exhausted'. Dashes and brackets also often contain definitions.
Antonym and example clues

An antonym clue shows a contrast. Signal words include but, however, unlike, instead and although. In 'Unlike her timid brother, Meera was audacious and loved adventure', we can guess that audacious means bold, the opposite of timid. An example clue lists examples of the word: 'Citrus fruits, such as lemons, oranges and limes, are rich in vitamin C.' From the examples we can tell that citrus fruits are sour, juicy fruits of the lemon family. Signal words include such as, for example, including and like.
General context and checking

Sometimes there is no single clue, and we must use the general sense of the sentence or paragraph. In 'After the long drought, the farmers were relieved when the rain finally came', we can infer that a drought is a long period without rain. It also helps to look at word parts: prefixes, roots and suffixes. Make your best guess, read on, and see if it still makes sense. Finally, check important words in a dictionary, because context gives an approximate meaning, and some words have several meanings that depend on the situation.
definitions: Context
The words and sentences surrounding a word that help explain its meaning.
Context clue
A hint in the surrounding text about the meaning of a word.
Inference
A conclusion reached using evidence and reasoning.
Signal words
Words such as 'but', 'such as' or 'means' that show the type of clue.
examples: Definition: A herbivore, an animal that eats only plants, has flat teeth for grinding.
Antonym: The first test was arduous, but the second was easy.

worked.problem: Work out the meaning: 'The old bridge was precarious; it swayed in the wind and looked as if it might collapse at any moment.'
steps: Look for clues after the semicolon: 'swayed', 'might collapse at any moment'.
These describe something unsafe and unstable.
Test the guess 'unsafe, likely to fall' in the sentence: it makes sense.
worked.answer: Precarious means unstable or dangerously likely to fall.

diagram.title: Types of context clues
rows: A nocturnal animal, one active at night…
Unlike lazy Raj, Anu was diligent.
Reptiles, such as snakes and lizards…

lessons.real_world: Readers of newspapers, novels and textbooks use context clues constantly. In competitive exams, reading comprehension sections test exactly this skill, and adults use it to understand legal, technical or medical documents filled with unfamiliar terms.
takeaways: Context clues help you guess meanings without stopping to look them up.
Look for definition, synonym, antonym and example clues and their signal words.
Use the general sense of the passage and word parts.
Confirm important guesses in a dictionary.
practice: Guess 'frugal': 'Being frugal, my grandfather never wasted food or money.'
Which signal word shows an antonym clue: 'such as' or 'unlike'?
What type of clue is in: 'Amphibians, such as frogs and toads, live on land and in water'?

EASY: The words around an unfamiliar word
Clues come from nearby words and sentences.
Which signal phrase usually introduces examples?
'A biography, the story of a person's life, …' This is a:
The phrase between commas defines the word.
Which word signals contrast (an antonym clue)?
MEDIUM: 'Unlike his garrulous sister, Amit hardly spoke.' Garrulous means:
Amit hardly spoke; his sister was unlike him.
The contrast shows garrulous means talkative.
'Many legumes, such as peas, beans and lentils, are rich in protein.' Legumes are:
plants whose seeds grow in pods
Peas, beans and lentils are pod-bearing plants.
'The room was immaculate; there was not a speck of dust anywhere.' Immaculate means:
What does 'not a speck of dust' suggest?
The clue shows it was spotless.
After guessing a word's meaning from context, you should:
Skip the rest of the passage
Check whether it makes sense and confirm in a dictionary if important
Test the guess and confirm important words.
HARD: 'The medicine alleviated her pain; within an hour she felt much better.' Alleviated means:
The pain lessened, so alleviated means reduced.
Which sentence gives a synonym clue for 'lethargic'?
Unlike the energetic puppy, the old dog was lethargic.
He felt lethargic — sluggish and slow — after the heavy meal.
Look for a word with a similar meaning.
'The scientist was sceptical of the claim and asked for more evidence.' Sceptical means:
Why would she ask for more evidence?
Why is context sometimes NOT enough to know a word's exact meaning?
Context may give only a general idea, and words can have several meanings
Context may be vague and words can be ambiguous.

topics.title: Letters and Notices
topics.description: Writing informal letters and school notices in the correct format.

lessons.title: Writing an Informal Letter
objectives: Identify the parts of an informal letter
Use an appropriate friendly tone
Organise content into clear paragraphs
Write an informal letter on a given topic
lessons.intro: In an age of text messages, a handwritten letter is still a special way to share news, thank someone or offer comfort. An informal letter is written to people we know well, such as family members and friends. It is warm and personal, but it still follows a clear structure so that the reader can enjoy it easily. Many examinations ask students to write informal letters.
sections: Format

An informal letter has these parts. (1) The sender's address, written at the top left (or right), followed by (2) the date, for example 12 March 2026. (3) The salutation or greeting: 'Dear Grandma,' or 'Dear Rohan,'. (4) The body, usually in three parts: an opening paragraph that greets and states the reason for writing, one or two middle paragraphs with the main news or ideas, and a closing paragraph with good wishes. (5) The complimentary close, such as 'With love,' or 'Your loving granddaughter,'. (6) The sender's name. No subject line is needed.
Tone and language

Informal letters use a friendly, conversational tone, as if you are talking to the reader. You may use contractions (I'm, can't), questions ('How is your new school?') and personal details. However, the letter should still be clear, grammatically correct and well organised. Avoid text-message shortcuts such as 'u' or 'gr8'. Show interest in the reader by asking about them and responding to news they may have shared. Keep each paragraph focused on one main idea.
Planning and writing

Before writing, decide the purpose: inviting, thanking, congratulating, describing an event, giving advice or apologising. Note three or four points to include. For example, a letter describing a school trip could cover where you went, what you saw, the most enjoyable moment and what you learned. Use vivid details: instead of 'It was nice', write 'The view of the sunrise over the hills turned the sky orange and pink.' End warmly, perhaps inviting a reply: 'Write back soon and tell me about your holidays.'
definitions: Informal letter
A personal letter to family or friends written in a friendly tone.
Salutation
The greeting at the start of a letter, such as 'Dear Asha,'.
Complimentary close
The phrase before the signature, such as 'With love,'.
Contraction
A shortened form such as I'm for I am.

worked.problem: Plan a letter to your cousin describing your first visit to a science museum.
steps: Address and date at the top; salutation 'Dear Kavya,'.
Paragraph 1: greet her, ask about her exams, say you want to share an exciting trip.
Paragraph 2: describe the museum — the planetarium show, the robot gallery, the giant DNA model.
Paragraph 3: the best moment and what you learned; suggest visiting together.
Close: 'Love, Arjun'.
worked.answer: A three-paragraph letter with address, date, greeting, vivid details, a warm ending, close and name.

lessons.real_world: Personal letters and emails to relatives abroad, thank-you notes after receiving gifts and letters of encouragement to friends all follow this pattern. Well-written personal letters are often kept for years as treasured memories.
takeaways: Informal letters go to people we know well.
Include address, date, salutation, body, complimentary close and name.
Use a friendly tone, but avoid text-message language.
Plan the purpose and points, and use vivid details.
practice: Write a suitable salutation for a letter to your best friend Meera.
Does an informal letter need a subject line?
Give one way to end an informal letter warmly.

EASY: An informal letter is usually written to:
Informal letters are for people we know well.
Which is a suitable salutation for an informal letter?
Which part comes at the very end of the letter?
The letter ends with the complimentary close and your name.
An informal letter does NOT need a:
Subject lines are for formal letters.
Informal letters do not have a subject line.
MEDIUM: Which sentence best suits an informal letter?
I am writing to lodge a complaint.
I'm so excited to tell you about my trip!
This sentence has a warm, personal tone.
Which should be avoided in an informal letter?
Text-message shortcuts are not suitable even in informal letters.
The opening paragraph of an informal letter should:
Greet the reader and say why you are writing
The opening greets and introduces the purpose.
Which complimentary close suits a letter to your grandmother?
'Your loving grandson,' is warm and personal.
HARD: Which detail would make a description of a festival more vivid?
The whole street glowed with hundreds of clay lamps.
Vivid means appealing to the senses.
Specific sensory detail paints a picture.
Your friend has just moved to a new city. Which middle-paragraph idea is MOST relevant?
Your opinion of a cricket match last year
A list of your school timetable
Asking how she is settling in and sharing ways to make new friends
Responding to her news shows interest and keeps the letter focused.
Why should each paragraph focus on one main idea?
It makes the letter easy to follow
Ideas cannot be mixed in English
One idea per paragraph keeps the letter clear and organised.
Do write back soon and tell me all about your new school!
It asks the reader to respond.
It warmly encourages the reader to reply.

lessons.title: Notice Writing
objectives: Explain the purpose of a notice
Use the correct format of a notice
Include all essential details: what, when, where, who and how
Write concise notices within a word limit
lessons.intro: A notice is a short, formal piece of writing that informs a group of people about an event, announcement, instruction or lost and found item. It is displayed on a notice board or shared in a newsletter or group message. Because people read notices quickly while passing by, a notice must be brief, clear and complete. School examinations usually set a limit of about 50 words for the body.
sections: Format

A notice follows a standard layout, usually inside a box. At the top is the name of the institution, such as 'Green Valley School, Pune'. Below it is the word NOTICE, in capital letters. Then come the date (on the left) and a short, catchy heading that tells what the notice is about, for example 'Inter-House Quiz Competition'. The body gives the details. At the end are the signature, the name of the writer in capitals and their designation, such as 'Secretary, Science Club'. Notices are written in the third person or in a formal, impersonal style.
Content: the five Ws

A good notice answers the questions what (the event or announcement), when (date and time), where (venue), who (who may take part or whom it concerns) and how (how to register, whom to contact, what to bring). Include deadlines and contact details clearly. Avoid unnecessary descriptions, greetings or personal opinions. Use short sentences or bullet points for clarity. The tone is formal and polite: 'All students of Classes VI to VIII are invited to…' or 'Interested students may give their names to the undersigned by 15 July.'
Common mistakes

Common mistakes include forgetting the date or heading, writing in a chatty letter style ('Hi friends!'), leaving out the venue or deadline, and exceeding the word limit with unnecessary details. Another error is writing the notice for the wrong audience. A lost-and-found notice should describe the item precisely ('a blue steel water bottle with the initials A.K.') and say where it was lost or found and whom to contact. Always read your notice from the point of view of someone who knows nothing about the event: can they act on it?
definitions: Notice
A short formal announcement displayed to inform a group of people.
Heading
A short title stating the subject of a notice.
Designation
The official position of the person issuing the notice.
Word limit
The maximum number of words allowed, usually about 50 for the body.
examples: Signature block: (Signature) / ANANYA SHARMA / Head Girl

worked.problem: Write a notice as Secretary of the Eco Club inviting students to a tree-plantation drive.
steps: Institution: Sunrise Public School, Lucknow; then NOTICE; date: 20 July 2026; heading: Tree-Plantation Drive.
What/who: The Eco Club is organising a tree-plantation drive; students of Classes VI–IX may participate.
When/where: Saturday 25 July 2026, 8:00–10:00 a.m., school back garden.
How: Give your names to the undersigned by 23 July; wear old clothes and bring a water bottle.
Sign off: (Signature) RAHUL VERMA, Secretary, Eco Club.
worked.answer: A boxed notice with institution, NOTICE, date, heading, five-W body under 50 words and signature with designation.

diagram.title: Notice format
items: Body: what, when, where, who, how

lessons.real_world: Notices are used by schools, housing societies, offices and government departments every day: water supply interruptions, meeting announcements and exam schedules. Being able to write a clear notice is a practical skill for any club secretary, class representative or office worker.
takeaways: A notice is brief, formal and placed in a box.
Include institution, NOTICE, date, heading, body and signature with designation.
Answer what, when, where, who and how.
Stay within the word limit and avoid a chatty tone.
practice: List the five Ws a notice should answer.
What, when, where, who and how.
What is the usual word limit for the body of a notice?
Write a heading for a notice about a lost watch.

EASY: In capital letters near the top
In the middle of the body
It is a clear label at the top.
NOTICE appears in capitals below the institution's name.
Which is NOT needed in a notice?
Notices do not include chatty greetings.
The usual word limit for the body of a school notice is about:
A notice is usually displayed on a:
Many people need to see it.
Notices are put up on notice boards.
MEDIUM: It should state the subject briefly.
A clear heading names the event.
Which detail is MISSING from: 'A debate will be held in the auditorium. Interested students may contact the undersigned.'?
It does not say when the debate will take place.
All students of Class VII are requested to assemble in the hall at 9 a.m.
Hey guys, come to the hall!
I really think you'll love it.
It is formal, clear and gives time and place.
What should appear below the signature?
The name in capitals and designation
The writer's name and position identify the issuer.
HARD: Which is the best description in a 'Found' notice?
A black leather wallet with a bus pass, found near the canteen on 3 August
